summary: The Pediatric GFR (glomerular filtration rate) calculator turns the height, the serum Creatinine and more into GFR (Pediatric GFR). It is built for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Press Calculate for the answer; change a value and it steps off screen until you press again, so each edit can be judged on its own.

sections.title: How does the Pediatric GFR (glomerular filtration rate) calculator work?
sections.html:
The Pediatric GFR (glomerular filtration rate) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports GFR (Pediatric GFR) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the sex); then you type in the height, the serum Creatinine, the serum Cystatin C and the BUN.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as female and male. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in centimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in milligrams per deciliter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 3 supported units.
  • A number, expressed in mg/L.
  • A number, expressed in Mg/d l.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Pediatric GFR (glomerular filtration rate) calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

GFR=((413 ÷ 10) × height ÷ serum Creatinine)
GFR=((7069 ÷ 100) ÷ (serum Cystatin C ^ 931 ÷ 1000))
GFR=((199 ÷ 175) × (2 ^ 79 ÷ 1000) × (3 ^ 183 ÷ 200) × (5 ^ 21 ÷ 25) × (7 ^ 821 ÷ 1000) × (height ^ 179 ÷ 1000) × sex × (height ÷ serum Creatinine ^ 57 ÷ 125) × (1 ÷ BUN ^ 79 ÷ 1000) × (1 ÷ serum Cystatin C ^ 209 ÷ 500))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Creatinine, opening in milligrams per deciliter

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Pediatric GFR (glomerular filtration rate) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the height, the serum Creatinine and the serum Cystatin C — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Pediatric GFR (glomerular filtration rate) calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The 1 drop-down on this page offers a fixed list of cases. A value that is not on the list cannot be entered, and the nearest option is not always a good substitute.
  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Pediatric GFR (glomerular filtration rate) calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns GFR (Pediatric GFR), derived from the height, the serum Creatinine and the serum Cystatin C. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Pediatric GFR (glomerular filtration rate) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the height, the serum Creatinine, the serum Cystatin C and the BUN, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter height in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Height opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports GFR = 1. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Pediatric GFR (glomerular filtration rate) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
